newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: GOLF-Tataurangi failures paved way for success.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-Tataurangi failures paved way for success.

text.p: SYDNEY, Nov 18 - An unsuccessful year on the United States professional tour two years ago paved the way for Phillip Tataurangi's success in the Australian PGA championship, NZPA reported on Monday.
Tataurangi, 25, said what he'd learned in 1994 on the arduous US PGA tour delivered him a somewhat miraculous win on the unforgiving, windswept New South Wales Golf Course.

Tataurangi said he was criticised for tackling the US PGA in his first year as a professional. He didn't play well enough to retain his card and has spent the past two seasons on the second tier Nike Tour.
Next month he has a chance to regain his US tour card, and join Grant Waite on the lucrative circuit, if he can finish in the top 40 of 220 at a six-round final qualifying school in California.
"Playing the US tour was a great learning experience for me," Tataurangi said,
"Where better way is there to learn your trade as a first year professional than there?
"My win here is the fruit of that year -- I learned so much, most probably because I was playing so badly," he said with typical modesty.
"While some people were critical of that move -- and I didn't win much money and only made about 11 of 24 cuts -- I kept my eyes and ears open and learned all I could from the world's best players.
"All those experiences, good and bad, accumulate and were what helped me win this tournament."

Tataurangi, who was a late entry for the tournament on a sponsor's exemption, is the first New Zealander to win the Australian PGA and joins such greats as Hale Irwin, Seve Ballesteros and Greg Norman on the winners' list.

He has now won two professional tournaments in a month after winning a Nike Tour event in Washington last month and thought while he was playing the best golf of his career, it was no different to what he'd been doing in the past year.
"I've been hitting the ball and playing golf like this for the past 12 to 18 months and this last month is just the culmination of all the previous experiences.
"But now I don't make as many mistakes as I used to."
Tataurangi's final round 67 yesterday was mistake-free. He made five birdies and no bogeys and the few holes in the middle of his round where he had to fight to make par, he did so with class.
Throughout the final day, which featured an hour-long stoppage because of strong winds up to 65 knots, Tataurangi said he was battling for what he thought might be second place.
He started the day eight shots behind overnight leader Chris Gray of Western Australia but only two shots from second place.
"Quite frankly at the start of the day I thought I was playing for second place," Tataurangi said.
"I went out to play as hard as I could and it's amazing what can happen in 18 holes of golf.
"I had the time of my life out there today and it worked out that the score I shot was good enough to win the tournament."
He was helped by Gray, who shot a five-over par 77, dropping most of his shots on the front nine.
His fellow Western Australia Wayne Smith had a short stint in the lead after a run of five birdies and an eagle in 11 holes took him to 11-under for the tournament.
Even at that point, Tataurangi was four shots off the pace but Smith also collapsed, dropping five shots in six holes.

Australian veteran Rodger Davis then took over the lead at nine-under, courtesy of six birdies after he started at three-under. He was in the group ahead of Tataurangi, who joined him on nine-under with two holes to play.

However, Davis made bogey on the tricky par-3 17th, where Tataurangi saved par after missing the green on the front right hand side -- a chip to within 2m followed by a putt which curled around the cup before it dropped.
Even a pulled drive into the car park on the last couldn't stop Tataurangi, who recovered with poise and almost sank a birdie putt.
Before he heads to California for the PGA Tour school, Tataurangi will play the World Cup of golf in Capetown, South Africa this weekend. He will be joined by Paul Devenport in the two-man Kiwi team.

New Zealanders took a fair chunk of the $A400,000 ($NZ448,329) PGA championship prize-money. Tataurangi picked up first prize of $A72,000, Michael Long earned $A9400 for a share of ninth place at two-under par, Steven Alker tied for 13th for a $A5800 payday.
Waite, after almost missing the cut on Friday, was tied for 35th ($A2000), Marcus Wheelhouse was equal 53rd, Devenport 70th and Elliot Boult 73rd.
Most of the New Zealanders now play the Australian Open here this week, which will feature American sensation Tiger Woods.
